newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's M1 up a sharp 3.0 percent in February.
newsitem.headline: Israel's M1 up a sharp 3.0 percent in February.

text.p: Israel's M1 money supply grew by a preliminary 3.0 percent in February to 18.09 billion shekels in its second sharp month-on-month increase, the Bank of Israel said on Sunday.

Money supply rose by a cumulative 6.47 percent in the first two months of 1997, following a 3.4 percent rise in January. In all of 1996, M1 grew 11.9 percent. On a year-on-year basis, money supply rose 18.2 percent in February.

A Bank of Israel official said the central bank believed falling inflation has been the "dominant factor" in the accelerating money supply growth. Inflation declined from a 14.6 percent annualised rate in first-half 1996 to 6.8 percent in the second half.

However, the consumer price index (CPI) released on Friday showed a sharp 1.2 percent increase in February from January. The figure was at the top end of analysts' expectations, and most said they expect high CPIs in coming months as well.

The central bank has spent an estimated $2.7 billion buying foreign currency this year to support the currency basket to which the Israeli shekel is officially linked. But officials said they have successfully absorbed the resulting liquidity.
Total credit grew 1.6 percent in February to 261.9 billion shekels, following a 1.9 percent increase in January. In February 1996, total credit grew 1.2 percent, the Bank of Israel said.
Unlinked-shekel lending contracted by 1.7 percent to 82.2 billion shekels following a 3.0 percent January rise, it added.
Money supply is one of the factors the Bank of Israel uses to determine interest rates. The central bank is due to announce its April monetary programme, including interest rate levels, on March 23.
